title: Shipping: The EU ETS and the Energy Complex
summary: The EU ETS continues to impose escalating costs on shipping, with carbon allowances now averaging €83.30/tonne, driven by volatile gas prices and increased demand for carbon-intensive power generation. This market dynamic, where higher gas prices make coal more competitive, highlights a systemic failure to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels, impacting shipping's operational expenditures directly. Despite these rising financial pressures, the industry's actual decarbonization efforts, especially among the dirtiest vessels, remain woefully inadequate to meet urgent environmental targets.
content:
The EU ETS is expected to keep impacting shipping both in the near and in the long term, following the latest gas price increases.

In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “the EUA market maintained its upward trend in August, despite the quieter trading conditions and lower liquidity that typically characterize the holiday period. The advance extended the recovery that began in late March and left the EU ETS on a constructive footing heading into autumn. The Front Dec-26 EUA contract averaged €82.36 /ton during August and at the time of writing read €83.30 /ton, around 6.5% above the 2026 y-t-d average. Prices remained within a relatively narrow range during the month, and the contract continued to trade above its 50-, 100- and 200-day moving averages. The European gas market has contributed to the firming of EUAs. Prices at the Dutch TTF hub rose significantly as geopolitical tensions leading to Qatari volumes off market, low European storage levels and competition from Asian buyers for LNG cargoes heightened concerns over winter supply”.

According to Intermodal’s Senior Analyst, Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, “although the correlation between front-month TTF gas prices and EUAs fluctuated in August, it has strengthened recently, suggesting that prevailing gas-market dynamics are supporting EUA demand. The principal transmission channel is fuel-switching economics: higher gas prices make coal more competitive with gas for power generation, encouraging more carbon-intensive output and increasing utilities’ demand for allowances. Furthermore, recent economic signals add to this supportive backdrop, pointing to firm industrial demand. The August eurozone manufacturing PMI reached its strongest level in more than four years, accompanied by stronger new orders, a recovery in exports and the first increase in factory employment after more than three years. Together, these developments strengthen the outlook for EUA demand”.

The shipbroker added that “despite the positive backdrop, traders remain cautious. Investment funds have reduced their net-long exposure in recent weeks, while commercial participants have continued to increase their forward exposure, reflecting hedging strategies built around expectations of further EUA price increases. The divergence indicates that commercial buying remains driven by risk management even as speculative interest weakens. Compliance buying adds another source of demand ahead of September 30, including from shipping companies as the maritime sector’s obligations continue to phase in. In 2026, shipping companies must surrender allowances covering 70% of their verified 2025 emissions within the scope of the EU ETS, rising to 100% of 2026 emissions in the following year, with higher EUA prices increasing the compliance cost of voyages covered by the scheme”.

“Looking ahead, policy is re-emerging as a major driver. The Commission’s July proposal for the post-2030 EU ETS would slow the contraction of the emissions cap, extend conditional free allocation and ease the operation of the Market Stability Reserve. The measures would leave more allowances in circulation than under the present framework, easing concerns about future supply constraints. The initial market response was positive, however, this is only the starting point for further negotiations, leaving scope for revision”, Mr. Tagoulis said.

He also noted that “beyond the EU ETS reform, the proposed linkage with the UK ETS remains an open issue. A summit expected to advance negotiations in July was postponed following the change in UK leadership, leaving the timetable uncertain. Progress towards linkage should narrow the spread between UKAs and EUAs as UK allowance prices move closer to EU levels. Once implemented, the linkage could become a bearish factor for EUA prices by expanding the pool of available allowances, although its impact would depend on supply conditions across both systems”.
